title: Olivia Cooke on her wild Slow Horses return, House of the Dragon's fans and overcoming burnout

 With killer roles in two of the best shows of the year, Olivia Cooke has never looked busier. But some burnout-enforced time off gave her perspective on toxic fandoms, social media – and what she wants to do next By Rebecca Dolan Photography by Elisa Baudoin 9 November 2026 Coat by Simone Rocha. Earrings by Sophie Bille Brahe. When I arrive at Olivia Cooke ’s local in Bethnal Green, it turns out she’s beaten me there, 10 minutes early. The pub is nearly empty at 5pm, but there's still atmosphere inside, low candles glowing red on tables and the ’70s soul croons of Rivage’s “I Need You Baby” in the background. “Some saloon in the middle of east London,” as Cooke puts it.
 She’s stationed in the back with a drink, looking impressively and almost intimidatingly put-together for a Monday evening, wrapped in a navy wool shawl. But within a few minutes, she's describing the “two welts on each bum cheek” she got from injecting shingles medication late last year, and we’re off.
 “I had a two-month period where I couldn’t do small talk. Someone was like, ‘How are you?’ and I was like, ‘Yeah, I’ve had shingles,’” she says, grinning a little as she recounts the migraines and rashes and post-jab marks.
 It was a special kind of hell for a self-described hypochondriac. The lurgy started at the end of last year, while she was staying at her House of the Dragon castmate Gayle Rankin’s house in upstate New York, after a back-to-back blitz of filming, reshoots, and press. She came back to London to get treated, and then took a six-month break that lasted until this June. “I feel like the past two years, I’ve been, like, jobs, jobs, jobs, and I got really burnt out,” she says. “Your body has a way of flooring you to make sure that you do actually lie down.”
 So the real-life Cooke , 32, spent most of this winter and spring cooped up at home with her partner Ralph Davis in their Victorian townhouse in east London (“I was like a real housewife, like, horribly, but I enjoyed it. I was cooking different meals every day and sorting my cupboards out”). But on screen, she was criss-crossing millennia and realms: plotting her escape from King’s Landing ( House of the Dragon ) and dodging gunfire in the English countryside ( Slow Horses ). This month, it’s the Dolomites and Rome, where she plays an American heiress pursued by a born-again Tom Ripley in A Talent for Murder .
 Apart from curly auburn hair and big, round eyes, Cooke’s signature is a kind of ease on screen. Her characters feel confident, fully saturated – even when she’s Alicent Hightower being imprisoned in a castle, or Sid Baker getting chased by Russian agents. “It’s highly social, but it’s easy,” she says of film and TV work.
 I question whether that’s really the case, especially when she says filming days usually mean 5am wake-ups, but she’s adamant: “You do have to be really on it. But also that’s just one of the five things that’s required of me, really. Know my lines, be on it, be awake. Maybe it’s because I’ve been doing it for 14 years. I look at the camera operator, and I’m just like, ‘Fuck me, that is hard.’”
 I believe in Cooke’s levels of chill after she admits that she took a secret holiday in the middle of filming HOTD last year. The schedule stretches seven months, but she was only actually needed for 40 days. “They didn’t know this, but I went to Spain for three weeks on holiday,” she says. “They thought I was in east London.” In reality, she was in Mallorca with her partner and friends, while they were filming a big battle scene that doesn’t involve Alicent. I ask if she thinks she could get away with that again next season. “Probably not, now that I've said it.”
 Her pluckiness clearly makes her characters feel more magnetic. She talks about someone screaming “Alicent!” at her while she was riding a Lime Bike recently, and the woman who came up to her in Clerkenwell after she finished a day of filming. “She just launched into a story like we’d been friends for years. I found it hilarious because she was just so unbothered. She was like, ‘Right, listen to me.’”
 This type of run-in happens more frequently now. In person, Cooke feels immediately approachable (later on, as soon as we stand up, someone comes up and asks her for a lighter). It does mean she has to be more “on high alert” when she goes out – part of why being actual Olivia, outside of a film set, feels harder. “I guess it’s just like, when do you really let the mask slip?” she wonders. “It’s Monday, so I’ve just been talking to my therapist about this.”
 A few months into her break, Olivia Cooke went for another kind of spring cleaning – deactivating all her social media accounts. “I was just like, I’m on this too much. It’s not nourishing,” she says. “I think the celebri-fied nature of being an actor has now snowballed into this monster. And I just think we need to get off this train and realise that we make these TV shows and films, yes, for escapism, but also because it’s artful and it’s creative and it’s not for followers or for a brand deal or to get free shit. Even though that is nice sometimes.”
 As of October, she’s now back on Instagram, but she still feels a bit removed from the algorithm-driven celebrity industrial complex. “Even replying to a DM from someone that is semi-famous or wholly famous, that’s anxiety,” she says. “I don’t know this person. It’s so weird. We might have had a nice interaction where we’ve liked each other’s stuff. But I don’t know. Why do I then now feel like I have to be smart and charming for this person that I don’t know?”
 Anxiety, whether about celebrity DMs or convincing herself she has early-onset Alzheimer's (“I am the boy who cried wolf every night”), is one of the things Cooke is most open about. She reckons that she’s “always had OCD”, but things got particularly bad when she was turning 22 in late 2015. She’d just moved to Brooklyn by herself, after filming Bates Motel . She suffered from panic attacks for three consecutive weeks and received a formal OCD diagnosis. “I wish I’d had someone I could confide in, who was like, ‘There are routes,’” she says. “I was so terrified of any medication whatsoever.”
 This year, she has spent a lot of her time off properly working on her mental health – not via the Goop-esque wellness world, which left her high and dry after half-hearted attempts at olive-oil shots and a vibration plate. The real breakthrough came after the long trial and error with antidepressants. She eventually landed on the correct dose, which she wishes she’d started a lot sooner. “I’ve got a chemical imbalance in my brain,” she says. “It’s taken me a while to get my head around that.”
 Cooke says House of the Dragon ’s third season dropping in summer was part of what drove her offline. The Game of Thrones prequel comes with a famously zealous, sometimes vicious fanbase. The controversial Queen Alicent gave them a lot to react to this season (a reluctant kiss with her own son, for starters, who later daydreams a scene where he has sex with his mum). Some turned their frustration on Cooke herself; others cast her as an unwilling victim of the directors. (“I genuinely feel bad for Olivia,” was one response from the Reddit chorus. “I hope she’s at least paid well.”)
 She tells me this is, in fact, bullshit. “I think some of those interpretations just catch fire, and they become something that bears no resemblance to what was shown on the screen at the time,” she says. “There's a lot of ugliness to that fandom as well. It’s steeped in misogyny. There’s a lot of racism. I try to let it take up minimal mental real estate.” The reality is that her relationship with director Clare Kilner is golden. She likes the fact that Kilner proves “you don’t have to stomp around the set and exert testosterone. You can just handle each department with kindness and care.”
 Cooke grew up in Oldham, just outside Manchester, which does, yes, make her relatively unique in the UK acting world (she was rejected by RADA and did without formal drama school training). But it grates on her that a lot of interviews labour the Northern point. "My mum, whenever an interview comes out – because… they only want to talk about the fact that I’m from a working-class background – she scoffs and she’s like, ‘ You’re fucking working class?’” Cooke says. “It pisses me off when someone assumes that someone from Manchester is working class when they’ve got an accent.”
 After seven-odd years living in London now, Cooke has to put the “rhino skin” back on her “soft baby Southern hands” when she goes home. You can tell, just from the mastery of Cooke’s sarcastic banter, that her Northern upbringing has armed her with a healthy degree of self-awareness about the weird business of being an actor. She credits her sense of humour to her hometown, where she says “not a sincere word is ever said.”
 Cooke thinks that people from Manchester have a complicated relationship with our new Prime Minister. She likes him – she rates a lot of what he did as mayor, and is cautiously optimistic when we speak in September, but “just with Labour at the moment, I’m not in love,” she says. “I think the way they’ve handled the genocide in Palestine has been horrendous, really. And quite sly, just lacking in any morality.”
 A lot of her best mates today are from her amateur theatre days back in Oldham. Her sister is younger than her, but already married with kids. She’s “very glamorous”, Cooke says. She actually based her character in The Girlfriend on her sister's style: “Nails, the lashes, the whole face every day, the blowout.” Her sister’s reaction? “‘Best you've ever looked.’”
 She takes another sip of her alcohol-free pilsner. She’s feeling the effects of being in her 30s more now. "Even tequila, I'll be in bed with the jitters. I'm too sensitive." So her social life leans a bit wholesome. There are dinner parties with friends, and “taking the sea air” on group trips. "Very Victorian.” A lot of her friends have kids, which changes things, but "it's gorgeous and it's so life-affirming at the same time."
 Cooke has been with her partner, Ralph Davis, for a few years – he played Ser Leon Estermont in season two of HOTD . Her highlight of this year was a week with him in Cornwall, where they had zero mobile service. I ask whether it ever gets competitive at home, since they spend so much of their time talking about acting, watching shows and plays and hanging out with all their actor friends. “[Ralph’s] just such a cheerleader, and it's really lovely,” she says. “He’s a writer as well, and he’s just as successful in that field as he is with his acting. So he’s got a bit of both.”
 I press her on whether she feels like she’s still having real fun these days, after all the soul-searching of her time off. “In a different way,” Cooke says. “It does feel like a different time of life. A different season. Things are serious now. It’s proper adulthood. I have to be just incredibly focused and good because there’s only me and I can't fall back on anything. I think that’s always been the case, but now I think I've not got the recklessness of youth to be like, ‘Everything’s going to be fine, whatever.’”
 When we meet, I’ve just finished season six of Slow Horses , where Cooke finally returns as Sid Baker, presumed dead since season one. I’m curious if Sid is the most Cooke-like character we’ve seen. She has a similar sense of humour, at least, and maybe the same kind of groundedness. “She’s definitely more steely than me,” Cooke says. “My poker face is non-existent.”
 She gushes, for a solid 10 minutes, about the vibe on the set of Slow Horses – director Adam Randall had to tell her to stop smiling when she was filming scenes where she’s being chased. “If there was just a pure, cold transcript of what is said during the day, you’d be like, ‘999, call the police,’” she jokes. “Will Smith wrote The Thick of It , one of my favourite shows, and he just has so much of that for free. And so that is the tone that is carried over and the environment and the culture of the set where everyone is ripping the piss out of each other.”
 This season, she only actually filmed scenes with Jack Lowden ’s River Cartwright, which made it feel like they were on an independent movie together. There’s a lot of sexual tension and banter between them, once again. But, finally, the two of them actually kiss, which was fully improvised. “There’s been such a crescendo to this moment, and these people are so limerent for each other, and they’re so sparkly when they’re around each other. It just felt like, this is the moment.” She is, for obvious reasons, team Jack Lowden for James Bond . “It’d be great if he got it,” she says. “I think he’d make an excellent Bond.”
 It’s left unclear at the end of season six of Slow Horses whether Cooke will be back for another (my money is on yes). The final episode sees River come home and then immediately get Novichok’ed, collapsing to the ground, while the shower is running upstairs and we know Sid is in the house. My own read was that it might be Sid herself who jabs him, since there are some hints throughout the season that she may not be as trustworthy as we think. “That didn’t even occur to me,” Cooke says, so I know I’m off the mark. “This is supposed to be Sid’s happy ever after.”
 This month, finally, the last of what she filmed during 2025 is coming out. Cooke didn’t actually meet Helen Mirren, who plays Patricia Highsmith in A Talent for Murder , until after filming, as she only had scenes with Alden Ehrenreich . “I adored working with him – someone, as well, who can take the piss out of themselves and wears it very lightly,” she says. Ehrenreich plays a young literary agent sent from New York to convince an ageing Highsmith, ensconced in the Swiss Alps, to write a new Tom Ripley book. It’s a completely fictional plot, based on the 2014 stage play Switzerland by Joanna Murray-Smith. Cooke liked that the film’s director, Anton Corbijn, didn’t micromanage them: “There was sort of implicit trust with Anton, which is a great confidence booster, when someone’s just like, ‘No, you go, fly.’”
 Like so many actors, she does see herself directing one day. A lot of her time off was spent leaning into what she calls her “creative season of life” – reading big history books (“A great one called Papyrus , which is about the history of the written word”), getting out of London and going to the theatre, which she wants to try herself again soon. “It’s so muscular, and it’s such a challenge,” she says. (She also, in fairness, made some time for The Real Housewives ).
 She thought a lot about the ways she could seek out culture, rather than having it foisted on her via her phone and algorithm. “It’s like the Youth Olympics at the moment,” she says. So she spent some time thinking instead about, “What do I want my 32-year-old womanhood to look like? Not be so navel gaze-y and not focus on wrinkles. I’m so bored, honestly, I’m so drained by that chat.”
 Now, the break is officially over. Cooke admits it wasn’t technically total freedom, since she had reshoots throughout. But she’s easing back into the intensity of red carpets and press junkets. “The amount of shit that I have to say no to because they want me to do embarrassing sketches or weird things,” she says. “I’m being glib, but I am a bit more withering. I’ve gotten older about all that shit.”
 She’ll hold on to the post-time-off glow as long as she can. She feels, as she puts it, “fantastic” – even if her younger sister likes to remind her that she’s in her 30s, unmarried and childless. “She thinks I’m going to be a rich old spinster,” Cooke says, finishing her drink. “But 32 is like a London 24.”
